title: Growing turnips
subtitle: A quick root crop and useful brassica for summer tops and winter roots
excerpt: Turnips are sown direct from March to July. Early sowings produce golf-ball sized summer roots; later sowings give larger roots for autumn and winter. The leafy tops of young plants (turnip tops or greens) are also edible, giving two crops from one planting.
sourceNotes: RHS turnip growing guide (rhs.org.uk). Mrs Beeton, Book of Household Management (1861), root vegetable section. USDA cooperative extension notes on turnip production, public domain.

glossaryTerms.definition: The young leafy tops of turnip plants, harvested when 10 to 15 cm tall as a cut-and-come-again leaf vegetable. Also called turnip greens. A nutritious and fast-growing alternative to spinach or chard. Sow turnips specifically for tops at high density (3 cm apart) in August or September and cut with scissors as needed; the roots are left in the ground.

content.text: Turnips mature quickly: summer varieties sown in March are ready in May, about eight weeks after sowing. Later sowings from June onwards produce larger roots for autumn and winter.
are a bonus crop available from any sowing. Milan Purple Top and Snowball are good early varieties; Golden Ball stores well for winter.

Sow direct in the growing position; turnips dislike transplanting. For a succession of summer roots, sow every three weeks from March to June, 1 to 2 cm deep in rows 23 to 30 cm apart. Thin in two stages to a final spacing of 15 to 22 cm. For autumn and winter roots, sow July or August. Cover seedlings with fine mesh against flea beetle.

Full sun to light shade. Any reasonable garden soil; turnips are not fussy. Avoid freshly manured ground, which produces forked or overly large leafy plants. Water consistently in dry spells; irregular moisture causes woody, pithy roots. Rotate with other brassicas on a three to four year cycle.

Pull summer turnips when golf-ball to tennis-ball sized for the best flavour and texture; they become woody if left much longer. Autumn and winter roots can stand in the ground until needed, lifted from September onwards. A light frost sweetens them slightly. Lift and store in sand in a frost-free shed if hard frosts are forecast.

attrs.heading: Common problems
attrs.intro: The main turnip problems in UK growing.

items.symptom: Tiny holes all over seedling leaves, plants growing slowly
items.fix: Cover with fine insect-proof netting from sowing. Water seedlings in dry weather to keep them growing vigorously past the vulnerable seedling stage; flea beetle damage is worst when growth is slow.

items.cause: Left too long before harvest, or irregular watering causing rapid growth spurts.
items.fix: Harvest summer turnips promptly. Water consistently.
